p.t: In short
Every email needs **one** call to action (the single thing you want the reader to do). Do not add several.

The email's job is to get the **click**. The full sales talk goes on the website.
Write the subject line and the body copy separately.

Use a **button** for the main action, and text of at least **14 point** (point = unit of text size).
Add a backup name like **'there'** so an empty first name never leaves a blank greeting.
Start with **text-led emails and only a few images**. Plain emails are more likely to reach the main inbox.
Before launch, **replace every placeholder** and **send a test** of each email in the flow.
Do not design emails yourself unless you have real design skill. **Use reusable blocks** instead.

Keep the **same design in every email** so readers know who is writing.
Each email has **one job**: get the reader to click through to the website.
Keep all brand files in **one permanent project**. Files in a one-off chat disappear when it closes.

Build in order: brand rules first, then email templates, then campaigns.
Set up the workspace **once**, and always start new chats inside the project.

Never paste an email as one **raw code block**. Keep it editable in Klaviyo.
**Test** every template on phones, in dark mode and in major email services before you use it.
Copy structure and purpose
An email has two parts: the **subject line** (the title the reader sees first) and the body copy (the main text). Write and improve each one separately.
Marketing emails that aim to get the reader to visit the site need copywriting (persuasive writing). Their purpose is to push the reader toward one **specific action**.
Direct selling emails start from **one** core problem of the target market (the group of buyers you sell to). The product is positioned to solve that problem.
Named structures for writing these emails include Problem-Agitate-Solution (name the problem, make it hurt, offer the fix), the Bencivenga persuasion equation (a persuasion formula)

and AIDA (Attention, Interest, Desire, Action).
The body copy of a marketing email has **one** job: generate clicks to a destination (the page the link opens).
The body copy must not sell inside the inbox (the reader's email app).
Persuasion, full proof and purchase decisions belong on the website. The website has room for images, videos and complete copy.

If an email tries to make the **full** sales case, readers who are not yet convinced do not click.
The store then loses the chance to convert them (turn them into buyers) on the site.

Send traffic straight to the website, where the full picture can be shown.
Do not answer the question or problem raised in the email.
Tell the reader they will learn the answer through the click. Otherwise there is no reason to take the action.
Email shares many similarities with content (articles, guides, posts).
Knowing customers' experiences, problems and pain points (problems that hurt) lets email address them more effectively.
Email marketing built on this research communicates more precisely with the customer.
The strategies that work in email are rooted in direct mail marketing (letters and postcards sent by post).
These strategies have stayed consistent for decades because human psychology has not changed.
Tested direct mail principles can therefore be applied to email copy and sequencing (the order of your emails).
Treat every email as a potential reusable template (a ready-made pattern you can copy).
Copy structure and purpose (continued)

Once an email is written, **reuse** it across other flows instead of writing from scratch. A flow is an automatic email series.
Reusing saves **significant time**.
Message matters more than format. Postage cost and fancy stationery do not increase response.
The **offer** and the **opening sentences** do increase response.
The six power reasons customers buy:
1. **Ownership:** use language and lifestyle images (photos of the product in everyday life) to make them feel they already own it. Use the car salesman technique: give control and choice.
2. **Logic:** identify the right customer, answer why it is relevant, and confirm it solves their specific problem.
3. **Social Proof** (other people's trust signals): include testimonials (written praise from customers), reviews, ratings and credible endorsements (recommendations from trusted people).

**Scarcity and Urgency** (making the offer feel rare and time-limited): use a limited-time offer, limited stock language, show others buying, and highlight the cost of inaction (what the reader loses by doing
nothing).
5. **Reciprocity** (people want to give back when they receive something): frame the offer as a gift (free shipping, discount), create obligation, and provide value first.
6. **Status:** identify the status the customer wants (luxury, eco-friendly, athletic) and position the product to align with and elevate that status.
Decide the call to action (CTA) **before** writing the body copy.
Typical CTAs in a copy email are learning more about a product, reading a blog post or downloading a lead magnet (a free download given in return for an email address).

Write the body copy **after** the subject line.
The body copy must follow on from the subject line's promise.
Together they should create curiosity. The body reveals only enough to make the reader want more.
Body copy formula
Email body formula for e-commerce copy emails, in order:
1. Greet the reader and confirm the problem that the CTA will help them solve.

2. Tease the solution, which is the product's primary promise (main promise) or the answer the content provides.
3. Explain at least one benefit of taking the CTA.

4. Offer the CTA.
5. Sign off.
After the subject line, briefly name the **primary** value or benefit the reader gets by taking the CTA.

Do not explain the whole content in the email.
For a content CTA, one primary benefit is usually enough.
If there are several, list **up to three** primary benefits. Keep each one short, because the content itself delivers the detail.

For a product CTA, focus the email on the product's primary promise.
If the product copy already has a clear primary promise, reuse that promise in the email.
Open the email body with a **short greeting** that also introduces the sender. The reader then knows who is writing before the problem is named.
Confirm the problem by pointing to how often customers ask about it. For example, say the store receives many emails or questions on the topic.
This makes the problem feel recognised and real before the solution is teased.
Name the destination in the email, such as a blog post, guide, product page or download.
This avoids surprising readers when the page asks for something other than a simple read.
This matters most when the link leads to an opt-in download (the reader agrees to receive something by giving their email).
A copy email for e-commerce should be **a few hundred words** in four or five short paragraphs.
Longer formats are used by digital product, consulting and coaching businesses. Typical e-commerce stores that send traffic to a full site do not need them.
A complete copy email follows the problem, solution, benefit and CTA formula. With two benefits and one guide link, it can run about **145 words**.
Body copy checklist

Body copy format checklist, in order:
1. Use a minimum font size of 14 point or larger.

2. Use short, simple sentences in easy-to-read language.
3. Use short paragraphs of one to two lines, and single-line paragraphs are common.

4. Make the CTA or links stand out.
5. Use only one CTA per email.
6. Use a personalised signature.

Sign emails with a **real person's name**, either the owner or a team member.
Do not sign with a generic business name or the word "Team".
Emails that feel personal, from a person to a person, tend to get better response rates.
Focus most emails on **exactly one** call to action.
p.h: One CTA, placed in several spots

p.t: Mixing several offers or links in one email reduces the response to each of them.
Several different CTAs overwhelm readers, lower interaction and often lead them to ignore the email and not return to it.
Adding many calls to action to one email reduces the number of clicks for each one.
Avoid daily-deal style emails (emails stuffed with many offers) unless that is actually your business model.
Several clickable elements in one email are acceptable if they all point to the same CTA and the same content.

Multiple different CTAs to different content should be avoided.
Place the one CTA in **several spots** that all lead to the same page:

a link within the sentence that names the topic,
a clear click instruction in the middle,
a link or button near the end.
These are multiple clickable areas for a single action, not several different offers.
Button or text link
Use a **button** rather than a plain text link for the main call to action.
Research cited here indicates that buttons improve click-through rates (clicks per reader) and action.

A CTA can be a clickable button or a standard underlined text link in a different colour, such as "click here to view".
Test both styles, since neither is proven to be better in general.
The two options differ. The button is the recommended default. The text link is an accepted alternative.
When you cannot tell which works better for your list, run both as a **test** (an A/B test: two versions, see which wins).
The call-to-action button must use a **unique colour** with strong contrast against the rest of the email. Examples: bright red, bright green or bright blue.
Any colour works, as long as the button clearly stands out.

Pattern:
A curiosity-driven subject line.
A greeting.
p.h: Pattern: problem, guide, two benefits, one CTA

p.t:
One sentence that names a common buying problem.
A sentence saying there is confusing information online.

A sentence promising a guide or resource that settles the question.
Two benefits the reader gets from clicking.
One repeated CTA with a clear link or button.
Why it works: the reader sees a problem they recognise, a promise of an answer and a **single clear next step**. So the click is the only logical action.
Example A (running shoes, subject: "Flat feet, which shoe?"): "Hi Sam, choosing running shoes with flat feet is a big decision.
Advice online contradicts itself on stability versus cushioning, so we wrote a short guide. Click here to see which features matter most and which model our fitters recommend for your stride."
Example B (mattresses, subject: "Firm or soft, which is right for your back?"): "Hi Lee, picking a mattress for back pain is not something to rush.
There are many mixed opinions about firm and soft, so we put together a simple comparison. Click here to see the pros and cons of each and which one our sleep team suggests for back sleepers."
Pairing a discount with a product
Pair the discount with **one** specific product suggestion in a single sentence. This links the saving to a second purchase.
This turns the coupon into a reason to add to the basket (shopping cart), rather than just a price cut.
Example 1: "Your 15% covers a second pair of socks, so add the matching cap while you are here."
Example 2: "Use your 15% on the refill pack and the saving pays for a travel size of the same cream."
Keep emails easy to scan (skim quickly).

Use one or two sentences per line, lots of white space (empty space) and no long paragraphs.
Readers scan first and read only what hooks them.

Short lines keep attention on the story and offer.
Use short, choppy sentences and short paragraphs of one to two lines.
Writing process for emails:
1. Write the basic structure of the email first, including the story beats (the key moments of the message) and the offer link.
2. Add the juicy details, emotional hooks (words that trigger feeling) and personality afterwards.
3. If writing is slow, dictate ideas into a phone recorder and send the recording to someone for transcription (turning speech into text).

Email body text for flows can be drafted with ChatGPT, but the draft still needs checking.
Before going live, confirm the links point to the **correct checkout and product pages**.

Also confirm that the wording matches the offer.
Small grammar errors are acceptable in emails.
Small errors can make the character more human and relatable.

Do not **delay sending** because of fear of mistakes. Consistent sending matters more than perfect text.
The flaw is part of the bond.
Keep a separate swipe file (a collection of saved examples) of emails collected from competitors and from marketers in other niches.
Use it as a source of ideas when you lack inspiration for your own email content. Do not copy it directly.
Font size and readability
Set the email body font to **at least 14 point** (pt = point, a unit of text size).
Automatic sizes of 12 or 10 point that many email tools produce are too small and hard to read for some people.

Body copy should use a minimum font size of **18 pt**, with up to 22 pt acceptable.
Bigger text is generally easier to read.

The two figures conflict. Use 18-22 pt for body copy where you can.
Treat 14 pt as the floor (the lowest allowed size) for copy emails.
Email content can use personalisation variables (placeholders that insert a reader's own details),

such as {{firstName}}.
Use a fallback value (a backup word used when the detail is missing), like 'Friend', for customers without a stored first name.

Personalise the greeting and subject line with the **first name**.
Adding the subscriber's first name makes the email feel more personal.

Add a default such as **'there'** to every personalised greeting and subject line.
Otherwise an empty first name in the profile leaves an empty greeting.
Personalisation in Klaviyo (an email tool; its template code is called Liquid) for the greeting and the subject line:
Greeting: Hey {{ first_name|default:'there' }}, Cart subject line: Still thinking it over, {{ first_name|default:'there'|title }}?

Use the fallback in both places, so an empty first name in the profile does not show up as a blank greeting.
The two fallback values differ. (,, )

'Friend' is the general personalisation fallback for variables.
'there' is the greeting and subject fallback used in the Klaviyo flow templates. (, )

Use 'Friend' for general content variables.
Use 'there' where the greeting reads "Hey there,".

The placeholder syntax (the exact code format) also differs between sources.
Klaviyo uses {{ first_name }}. ( shows it without a fallback, although requires one.)

Generic text uses {first_name} and {discount_code}, which you **replace yourself**.
Placeholder mapping in the flow templates:
Personalisation and dynamic content (continued)

{{ first_name }} and [NAME TAG] take the subscriber's first name from the Klaviyo profile.
[DISCOUNT CODE] takes the discount code of that flow.

[BUTTON] is a call-to-action button linking to the store.
[CART] is the block listing the products left in the abandoned cart (a basket left unpaid).

[BEST SELLERS] is a product block of top sellers.
[REVIEWS] is a block of customer reviews.
[TIMER] is a countdown.

[SIGNATURE] is the sender sign-off.
Dynamic content (content that changes for each reader) may not appear fully in email previews.
**Check the preview** of each campaign before sending.

Setting up the flows in Klaviyo:
1. Create or open the Klaviyo account.
2. Create the abandoned cart flow, the welcome flow and the post-purchase flow.
3. Load the ready-made team template for each flow into the matching flow. Use **one email per step**, in the order given below.
4. **Replace** every blank (______) and every bracketed placeholder with real store content, your real discount code and your real links.
5. **Check** the offer, the deadline wording and the review block in each email before turning the flow on.
Place the review block at the **end** of each email, after the call to action.

Reviews act as social proof and reinforce the decision without competing with the discount code.
Keep the stock line only if it is accurate.
Keep the 100% satisfaction line only if the store offers that guarantee.
Every flow email should show the brand logo and footer. Klaviyo takes these from the brand assets once they are set up.
A footer can also hold social media icons. They are added as their own section in the email builder (the editor where you design the email).
Claims, accuracy and launch checks
Vague superlatives are big claims with no proof, such as "150% more awesome. Made-up numbers count too.

**Remove them** unless they are real. Replace them with a specific benefit you can check. Only mention a guarantee that the store really offers in its return policy (the written rules for returns and refunds).
Blanks (______), placeholders such as [NAME TAG], [BUTTON], [REVIEWS] or [DISCOUNT CODE] are stand-in text. If you leave them in before launch, customers see them.
**Check a test send** of every email in the flow (a flow is an automatic series of emails) before you switch it on.
An email inside a flow that is still in draft status (saved, not active) is not sent. You can keep an unwanted email safe by leaving it in draft.

Before you use a bought email template, **check it on mobile** (phones) and in every email app (email client, such as Gmail or Outlook). Designs can look good on a marketplace page and still break in real inboxes.
HTML is the code that builds an email's layout. Plain text is an email with no layout code, just words.
**HTML is preferred over plain text, though the gap matters less than it used to.**

**HTML allows clickable buttons and a logo, so use it, but keep the layout simple.**
When it applies: When you need buttons and a logo.
**Simple text-based emails are preferred for small and medium e-commerce stores. HTML remains useful when images must be shown.**
When it applies: Small and medium stores; HTML when images must be shown.

**Write emails mostly as plain text with few or no images. The wording sells, and many email clients do not display images.**
When it applies: Default writing mode.
**Plain text emails that look like a message from a friend can perform well, even compared with heavily designed templates.**
When it applies: Any list used for many offers.
Positions in the Sources (continued)
**For a new store, start with text-led emails that use a few images, since they are more likely to reach the primary inbox. Compare open and click results in a test rather than relying on taste.**

When it applies: New stores; test to decide.
Heavily designed HTML emails are linked to promotional mailings. People do not usually write like that to each other.
Text emails with a few images are more likely to land in the **primary inbox** (the main inbox).
Image-heavy emails from the start risk the **Promotions tab** (Gmail's folder for marketing mail), where people open them less.
Heavy HTML may not display well in every inbox, device or email client. Some evidence suggests it is more likely to go to the Promotions tab or to **spam** (the junk folder).
Big stores often send three or four heavily designed HTML emails a day, full of offers. The author does not think this is the best approach for small and medium businesses.
A simple email with one **CTA** (call to action: the one thing you want the reader to do) does not need elaborate design.
There is no evidence that heavy design gets more **clicks** (click-through rate: the share of readers who click a link). Some evidence points the other way.
Too many decorations, images and colours is a mistake. Email providers may strip out part of the code, and the layout can break on some devices. The email may then look broken or make less sense.

**Build layouts with HTML and CSS** (CSS is the code that sets colours, fonts and spacing). Do not use image banners (one big picture holding the text). Images can be blocked, so the layout must work without them.
Include links to a few website categories in most emails. Readers who do not care about the email topic may still click through to the shop.
Email HTML is not normal web HTML. It still relies largely on 1990s-era techniques. Each email host renders the same design differently.
For example, Gmail, Yahoo and Hotmail show the same design in different ways.
**Design for the lowest common denominator**, meaning the simplest setup that works everywhere. Learn what each email client supports and does not support before you build.
Images, colour and visual layout
Klaviyo is the email software used in these examples.
**Use images sparingly.** Choose only the best product images, such as the product itself or the product in use. Many images raise the risk of spam placement and of formatting being stripped.
Heavy HTML can look like scam email. A product email benefits from one product image. Many email types need no images at all.
There is no reliable evidence that emails with images perform better than text-only emails. **Add an image only** when it serves the message, such as a product photo.
Choose your best product images, not decorative graphics.
A picture and short text can be combined into one image. For example, a collage of customer review screenshots can be made in Canva (an online design tool).
Place it as an image block (a single piece of an email) in a Klaviyo email.

In abandoned cart emails (emails sent to people who left items in their basket), this adds **social proof** (signs that other people trust you, such as reviews) without making the whole email an image.
Include pinnable product images, so subscribers can save products to **Pinterest** (an image-saving site) when they are not ready to buy.
This keeps the product visible and gives the customer a place to return to.
Put the text on a **white background** so it is easy to read. A text column with a coloured background on each side is fine, as long as the area behind the text stays white.

In a campaign email (a one-off email sent to a list), white is a clean base for product emails. Set the background colour in the editor's styling options. Add offers, text blocks and product feeds on top of it.
**Limit colours to your brand colours**, usually one or two main colours already used on the website. Use them when you need colour in an email.
**Use one email template for all emails**, so subscribers see a message and know right away that it comes from your brand.
Consistent design builds on trust that subscribers already have. Changing styles and layouts from email to email creates doubt about who is sending. Keep the design recognisable across all emails.
**Keep email design simple.** Most results come from strong copy, a clear message and an easy-to-spot call to action.
Klaviyo editor structure
The Klaviyo email editor builds content from sections and blocks. This works like editing a theme in Shopify (online store software).
**A button block cannot sit directly between two text blocks.** Add two text blocks and put the button between them.

In a campaign, **click Product > Create product feed**. A product feed is a list of products that updates itself. Show a collection, best-selling products or most-viewed products over a set period, such as 90 days.
This promotes your main products during an event.
The dynamic product section works the same way. Under Products, **click Create product feed**. Then choose best-selling or most-viewed products over a set time range, for example 90 days.
Email modules work like building blocks (ready-made pieces you can reuse).
p.h: Modular templates and content blocks: Building Blocks

p.t: **Stack them in any order** inside an email. The same modular approach works for both campaigns and flows.
A content block or module is one part of an email. A template is the full email built from those parts. A shared set of blocks and templates keeps campaigns and flows consistent.
**Build a set of reusable blocks** instead of one custom-designed email. You can then use the same blocks for every campaign and flow you send later.
Some modules, such as M19, are universal. Nearly every brand can use them. **Build these first** in a module library (a saved collection of modules).
With a ready module library, done-for-you clients (clients who pay you to build everything) can build an email in **three to five minutes**. They do not design each email from scratch.
All modules are tested on mobile and in dark mode (a display setting with a dark background). Emails built from them show correctly without extra checks.
Building from tested blocks gives quick, consistent results.
The always-on programme covers both campaigns and automated flows. It should stay editable in your email platform.
Sliced-image designs (a design cut into picture slices) look attractive but cannot grow into flows, and they break in real inboxes.
Module Library
An email module library holds **21 reusable modules**: 8 system modules (sage, a grey-green colour) and 13 content modules (terracotta,

a brownish-orange colour). Most emails are remixes of these modules.
**Header and footer**: Header (no nav), Header (with nav), Footer (no nav), Footer (with nav)

**Hero and imagery**: Image Hero, Big Number Hero, Announcement Bar
**Product**: Product Left, Product Right, 2-up Product Grid, 3-up Product Grid
**Conversion and trust**: Primary CTA, Promo Code Callout, USP Strip, Social Proof, Stats Row
**Text and structure**: Long form Text, Quote, Founder Sign-off, Section Divider, Thanks founder name
**Coded modules**: M5A, M5B, M8A, M8B, M9, M11, M12, M13, M14, M15, M16, M17, M18, M19
The Promo Code Callout module (a box that shows the offer) states the whole offer on one line.
That means a percentage discount, its scope and the code to enter, such as "20% off everything with code SAVE20. **Put all three together** so the reader sees the full offer in one block.

Editorial email template (a story-style email), in order:
1. Header
2. M11 module

3. A second M11 module with founder sign-off (the founder's closing note)
4. M12 module
5. Footer (the bottom section)

**Save the finished structure** as an editorial template. Clone it each time you need an editorial email.
Product showcase email template, in order:

1. Hero section (the large top image or big number)
2. Product Left
3. Product Right

4. Three-up product grid, with two of the products stacked on top of each other
5. Footer

Use this when no existing module fits.
1. **Describe the specific use case** to Claude.

2. Have Claude Design build the new module for that use case.
3. Upload the finished module to the module library.
Reusing one Klaviyo email design across a flow:
p.h: Reusing a design across a flow

p.t:
1. Build the first email from a pre-made template. **Edit the mobile version first.**
2. Click the arrow next to edit email, choose save as template, and name it after your store.
3. For each further email, click the arrow next to edit email, choose change template, drag and drop, open My templates, select the saved store template and click Use template.
4. Replace the text with your prepared copy. **Set the email from draft to live.**
Design method comparison
Email design methods are compared on two things:
**Programme fit**: how well the method suits running email at scale.
It covers editability (how easy it is to change later), render safety (whether it looks right everywhere) and scalability (whether it grows into flows).
**Design wow factor**: how impressive it looks.
Higher is better on programme fit. Higher on the right means more wow factor. Every method involves trade-offs, so no single option wins on every point.
The same comparison applies to other email platforms, such as Omnisend. The tool name changes. The trade-offs stay the same.
Marketplaces such as Envato and ThemeForest sell ready-made designs. Figma is a design tool for layouts. BeFree is a third-party tool for email design.

Klaviyo Composer is a new Klaviyo design helper, here in alpha (an early test version).
**Self-design in Canva or Figma**
Strength: Full control if you have real graphic and email design skill
Weakness: Easily looks amateur, can damage the brand, often abandoned after weeks or months

**Bought template (Envato, ThemeForest, similar marketplaces)**
Strength: Quick start, can look good on paper
Weakness: Often made by graphic designers, may be image-based, mobile and cross-client rendering often unverified

**Third-party tool (BeFree, later renamed LGE Studio)**
Strength: Polished, modular templates

Weakness: Two-tool workflow, pushed to Klaviyo as one large HTML block, every edit needs a re-push
**Professional designer file (Figma or Canva)**
Strength: Pleasing, professional look

Weakness: Delivered as locked images, text can be changed but layout and module order cannot, does not scale into flows
**Klaviyo native editor**

Strength: Editable, render-safe, repeatable
Weakness: Needs patience and skill to produce polished design
**Klaviyo Composer (alpha at time of lesson)**

Strength: Expected to allow better native, editable Klaviyo designs
Weakness: Still in alpha, full extent unknown
Design method comparison (continued)

**Modular system with reusable content blocks**
Strength: On-brand, editable, scalable for campaigns and flows
Weakness: Less polished than a bespoke designer look
**Only design emails yourself** in Canva or Figma if you have professional graphic and email design skills. If you lack them, avoid this route entirely.
Graphic design and email design are different skills. Email design depends on specific psychology and on where modules go. A graphic designer may not know this.
Founders who design their own emails without the right skills often spend weeks or months on it, then give up for another route. Self-designed emails can also do real damage to the brand.
BeFree, later renamed LGE Studio, is a third-party tool for building modular email templates and pushing them to Klaviyo. The result is **one large HTML block**.
Every change means going back to the tool and pushing again.
Professional designer files in Figma or Canva are usually locked images. Buyers can often change the text but not the layout, and the blocks do not stack in any order.
The Klaviyo native editor (Klaviyo's own builder) makes editable, render-safe emails. **It takes patience and design skill** to make the result look polished.

Klaviyo Composer was in alpha. It was expected to release publicly **within about one month** of when this was written. It is meant to help design better emails natively in Klaviyo while staying editable and scalable.
The modular system trades some visual polish for on-brand consistency, editability and scalability. It suits operators who send many emails and value speed over a custom look.
The modular email system is also a two-tool workflow, like a third-party tool setup. Its main advantage is reusable content blocks and scaling across campaigns. It is not a single-tool process.
The modular system is rated the most widely rendered option of the methods compared. It should work on mobile and in dark mode. It is chosen for scalability first, with polish second.
On programme fit, a modular system built with an AI approach and Klaviyo's native editor scores about equal. The sliced-image designer route may look more impressive.
But it breaks in real inboxes and cannot grow into flows.
**Choose a professional designer** if a fully custom look is the top priority, and you accept locked, non-editable files.
**Choose the modular system** if editability, consistent branding and scaling across campaigns and flows matter most.
Brand voice file
Markdown is a simple text format that uses symbols like # for headings. It is the most AI-friendly format for storing brand voice and style rules.

Language models (AI writing systems) can easily read, structure and use it when writing brand content.
**Fill in this brand voice template** for each brand:
# [Brand Name], Brand Voice ## Tone and personality description Write 1-2 sentences that capture the brand's communication style, personality,
and the emotional frame it uses to present its category.
Example: "Silk The Label speaks with a calm, aspirational tone that frames sleep as a luxurious act of self-care-blending functional product confidence with gentle,

wellness-driven warmth." ## Core voice attributes (integrate consistently) - [Attribute 1] - [Attribute 2] - [Attribute 3] - [Attribute 4] - [Attribute 5] ## Prohibited voice patterns (enforce as non-negotiable
rules) - [What to avoid, e.g., "Overly clinical or technical language"] - [What to avoid, e.g., "Loud, pushy sales tactics"] - [What to avoid, e.g., "Casual

or flippant tone that undermines the luxury feel"] ## Aesthetic and positioning framework Describe the sensory and linguistic character, the design philosophy, and the market position the brand occupies.
Example: "Silk The Label presents a refined, feminine luxury aesthetic built around soft jewel tones, clean typography, and aspirational lifestyle imagery.
Aesthetic markers: [descriptor words, e.g., "luxurious, minimal, feminine, elegant, serene"] ## Proven performance samples (accumulate over time) <!-- Collect subject lines
and openers that drive the strongest results as you run campaigns -->

After you write your voice file, **fill the Examples section** with real subject lines (the title line of an email) and email openers (the first lines) that performed well. Add new ones with each campaign.
This builds a live reference of how your brand voice works in practice. It stops drift into generic writing and gives AI-written content proven patterns to copy.
A **prompt** is the instruction you type to an AI tool. Ask the AI first for the best prompt for a writing task. Then use that prompt for the real copy.
This two-step approach should give stronger results than one generic request.
A campaign calendar (a plan of emails for weeks or months) can be generated **in one or a few prompts**. This saves a lot of time compared with writing each email by hand in Klaviyo.
A modular system built with an AI approach scores well on programme fit.
Flow body text drafted with ChatGPT (an AI chat tool) still needs checking. **Check it against the links and the offer** before launch.
Launch procedure for flows
1. **Create the flow** and load the matching template for each email, in the order given.

2. **Replace every blank and placeholder** with real store content, the real discount code and real links.
3. **Check a test send** of every email in the flow.

4. **Check the offer, the deadline wording and the review block** in each email.
5. **Turn the flow on** only when all emails pass.
an email has **one job**, which is to get the reader to visit the website.
p.h: Email body copy and calls to action

p.t: Trying to close the sale inside the message misses that job. The purchase decision belongs to the site.
**Length matters less** than whether each paragraph keeps the reader interested. Long copy can beat short copy when the reader is already interested. He will read several pages to learn more.

A short promotional email that produced a single tracked result used this structure:
1. The headline is used as the subject line.

2. Two or three one-line payoff sentences follow.
3. One big promise.
4. One quote from an authority figure (an expert or well-known person).
5. One link, as the only call to action.

The email showed no product details, so readers had to click to learn more. In that tracked campaign, **roughly 11 out of every 100 recipients clicked**. This is one result to watch, not a guaranteed benchmark.
**Place social proof right beside each unique value proposition** (USP: what makes your offer different), such as a review, a bestseller or a customer story.
Claims alone persuade less than claims shown with evidence.
**Remove text that repeats the header**, such as a brand name next to a logo. This keeps the email shorter and easier to scan.
Compose.ai is a tool for writing marketing emails. It helps when a store needs many email drafts without hiring a copywriter.
Brand colours in the email
**Keep text and background black and white.** Use only the brand colour for the button fill. The emails then match the store's look without distracting.
The Chrome extension "ColorPick Eyedropper" (a small add-on for the Chrome browser; also called "color picker") copies the six-digit hex code of any colour on a page.
A hex code is a six-character code that names one exact colour. You can paste it into Shopify's colour fields.
Keep the brand kit, tone-of-voice files, templates and campaign work in **one permanent project** that the AI can always reach.

Brand kit means your brand rules, such as colors and fonts.
Tone of voice means how your brand sounds in writing.
A project is a workspace where files and memory stay together.

Files in a one-off chat are lost when the chat closes. Then the AI guesses at the brand instead of using your real files.
Build the work in a **fixed order**. Do not skip ahead.

First: brand kit and tone of voice.
Second: email templates and universal content blocks built from them.

A template is a reusable email design.
Universal content blocks are reusable pieces of an email, such as an image or a button.

Third: campaigns built from both.
Each step reads the output of the previous one. So every file must sit in the same place.
A tidy project folder uses **numbered folders** for each stage. Examples: workspace setup, brand context, template from scratch, building campaigns.

Add a stack setup folder. A stack is the set of tools you use together.
Add an archive folder for older files.
Claude Cowork workspace setup
Workspace setup for Claude Cowork (the task mode of the Claude app that works on files on your computer)

and Klaviyo (email marketing software):
1. Download the **Claude desktop app** from **claude.com**. Install it like any other program.

2. Open the app. It starts on the Chat tab. Switch to **Cowork**.
3. Go to **Projects** and click **New project**. Then choose to start from scratch.
4. **Name** the project, for example Email Template Project. Optionally add a short description, such as "building email templates to push to Klaviyo. Push means send into your Klaviyo account.

No detailed instructions are needed.
5. Choose the **project location folder**. Then click **Create**.
6. Confirm that **Memory** is switched on. Memory means Claude keeps notes across all chats in this project.
7. Select the **model**. Opus, one of Claude's AI models, is used in this setup. Choose the **approval mode**, the setting for how often Claude asks you before it acts.
8. Create a **dedicated folder** inside the project location. Put all downloaded course files into it.
9. **Always** start new chats from inside the project. Never start from a standalone chat or a new Cowork task.

**Creating a project:** In Cowork, go to **Projects**, click **New project**, and choose to start from scratch. Give it a name and a short description. Choose the project location folder and click **Create**.
The Memory toggle (an on/off switch) is in the same dialog and must be **on**.
The **project instructions** field is optional. A short line of context is enough to start. For example: building email templates to push to Klaviyo.
Project memory must be **switched on**. Then Claude keeps the conversation history across all chats in the same project. Without it, you must re-explain the brand and background in every new chat.

A project page has three sections.
**Instructions** holds your project rules.
**Context** holds files. Add them with the plus button.

**Memory** lets you ask Claude to remember something.
All chats started in the project appear there, with their history.
The workspace setup takes about **five minutes**, and you do it once. If you skip it, the AI loses access to the brand kit and image files. It then starts guessing at the brand.
Installing and using skills

A skill is a saved set of instructions that Claude can run.
Installing a skill:

1. Go to **Customize > Skills**.
2. Click the **plus button**. Choose **Create skill**, then **Upload skill**.
3. Drag the skill files you downloaded into the **upload window**.
4. **Wait** a few seconds, until the skill shows as installed and ready to use.

To run a skill in Cowork, type the **slash character (/)** in the chat input. A list of installed skills and the file picker (the window for choosing files) appears. Select a skill and press **Enter**.

It starts without any extra prompt.
The **email builder skill** creates email templates. They are pushed to Klaviyo as editable templates.

The **campaign studio skill** creates campaigns directly inside Cowork.
The output appears in your Klaviyo account.
**Universal content blocks** are reusable email building pieces.
p.h: Modular content blocks and master template

p.t: A set of them, with a **master template** (one shared base design), lets the same pieces power welcome flows, campaigns and one-off sends.

A welcome flow is an automatic email series for new subscribers (people on your email list).
A campaign is a one-time email to a list.

Templates built this way stay consistent across all sends.
Universal content blocks are made with the **email template builder skill**. It needs these inputs:

Two reference images: an anatomy image and a module library image.
**brand-kit.json**, your brand kit saved as a JSON file (a plain text file with a fixed structure).
The output is a set of blocks and a master template. These are pushed into Klaviyo.
Once universal content blocks exist in Klaviyo, new emails are fast to build. Just **swap images** and reorder a few modules. Every send looks consistent.
After the foundation stage (universal content blocks and master template), you can stop and use working templates.
These cover **sales postcards** (short promotional emails), product showcases and editorial emails (emails that read like a magazine article).
Later stages only add flows (automatic email series), audits (checks) and segmentation (sorting subscribers into groups).

Do not push an AI-written email into Klaviyo as one large **raw HTML** block. HTML is the code behind an email.
Raw HTML cannot be edited in Klaviyo.

To change it, you must export it again.
Push templates and universal content blocks as structures that stay editable in Klaviyo.
AI-assisted build sequence

Planned sequence of the AI email build:
1. Set up the **tech stack** and install all tools.

Claude Cowork.
Klaviyo MCP. MCP is a connector that lets Claude work inside another app.

Brandfetch MCP, a connector that pulls brand details such as logos and colors.
Optional image tools.
2. Create a **brand context document** from the brand kit. It holds brand-kit.json with voice, colors and fonts.
3. Build the universal content blocks and master template with the **email template builder skill**. Then **push them into Klaviyo**.
4. Build **flows**, such as the welcome flow, using the same blocks. Then **map the flows**, meaning draw a diagram of each one.

5. Run an **email deliverability audit**. Deliverability means whether emails reach the inbox and not the spam folder.
Check Gmail, Hotmail and Yahoo accounts.
You need **DNS access** to the brand domain. DNS is the set of settings that control your domain's email rules.
6. **Audit** your Klaviyo send data (records of what was sent and how people responded). Then build **audience segments**, which are groups of subscribers.
7. Create a **campaign calendar** (a schedule of planned sends) with the email strategy planning skill. Feed it into Klaviyo.
8. Optionally add **SMS opt-in flows**. SMS means text messages. Opt-in means people agree to receive them. You can also add copywriting, which means the written words.
The AI-to-email stack changes **very fast**. Re-check specific tools and workflows regularly.
Klaviyo is releasing its own AI composer tools (AI tools for writing emails). These will change the workflow.

Campaigns made by the campaign skill are saved in Klaviyo as **drafts**. A draft is an unsent version. It is not live.
Review and schedule it inside Klaviyo.
Welcome flow

Welcome flow design uses three tools.
**Excalidraw**, a drawing tool for flow maps.

Claude Cowork with the Klaviyo MCP.
The email flow builder skill.
The inputs are brand-kit.json and the master template.
The target result is **one live welcome flow** and four flow maps.
Email templates must **render** well. Render means how the email looks on screen.

Test in major email services such as Gmail, Yahoo and Hotmail.
Test on mobile devices (phones and tablets).

Test in dark mode (light text on a dark background).
Test each template across all of these **before production use**, which means before it goes live.
The hero image is the large main picture at the top of an email.
p.h: Hero image, layout and links in Klaviyo

p.t: Use a welcome email hero image of **1250 x 2335 px**. px means pixels, the unit for image size.

Check the file quality after downloading and before uploading.
Blurry images reduce trust.
Check the hero image's dimensions and file size in the **file properties** before uploading.

The example welcome hero measured **1250 x 2335 px at 309 KB**. KB means kilobytes, the unit for file size.
It looked sharp at that size.

Set the **top padding** of the email content block to **30 px**. Padding is empty space inside a box.
It keeps the first element off the top edge.

A text block that is not full width on mobile is acceptable for this layout.
Edit the hero image in Klaviyo's email builder (the editor where you design emails).

Select the **hero image block**.
Choose **Upload image**.
Drag the file in to replace the old one.
Hero image, layout and links in Klaviyo (continued)
The Image block settings include: Link address (the web address a click opens), Image size with **Width set to auto**, Fill column on mobile, Alignment, Background color, Border, and Padding.
**Preview** the email before saving. Confirm that the image and padding look right on desktop and mobile.
To link an email or SMS button to a bestseller page on most **Shopify** stores (an online store platform):
Open **storedomain.com/collections**. It shows the store's pre-built collection list (groups of products).

Open the **bestseller collection** (the top-selling products).
Copy its URL into the **link field**.
In the greeting, insert the **first_name** profile property. A profile property is a stored detail about a subscriber.

Add a **default fallback**. A fallback is backup text used when the name is missing.
Subscribers without a stored name still get a natural opening line.

Open **Preview profile info** to see the greeting with a real subscriber profile.
Do this **before going live**.
To prevent **image distortion** (stretched or squashed pictures) in Shopify email templates on mobile:

1. Click the **Mobile Preview tab** while editing the email.
2. Check how images render on mobile.

3. Select each image and add **padding**, typically **10 pixels** on each side.
4. This gives space between images and the email borders.
A template must work on **mobile**, in **dark mode** and across all major email services before you use it.
Image-only emails (emails made only of pictures) are a poor choice.
Avoid them if you need **scalability** (the ability to grow without rebuilding) and **programmability** (the ability to control the email with rules and code).
